reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal track lined by granulation tissue connecting the anal canal or rectum to the perianal skin, usually the sequel of a drained or spontaneously discharging anorectal abscess
Typical symptoms are recurrent perianal discharge, intermittent pain and swelling that flares when the external opening blocks, and pruritus, often with a history of a previous abscess
The Parks classification describes tracks in relation to the sphincters as intersphincteric, transsphincteric, suprasphincteric, and extrasphincteric
Goodsall rule helps predict the internal opening: anterior openings tend to track radially, while posterior openings tend to curve to a posterior midline internal opening
MRI of the pelvis and endoanal ultrasound accurately map complex tracks, secondary extensions, and the relationship to the sphincter complex before surgery

The therapeutic balance is eradicating the fistula while preserving continence; low simple tracks may be laid open, whereas tracks involving significant sphincter muscle need sphincter-preserving techniques or a seton
Recurrent, multiple, or complex fistulae should raise suspicion of Crohn disease, tuberculosis, or malignancy and prompt appropriate investigation
reference.pathophysiology: Most fistulae-in-ano arise from the cryptoglandular theory: infection of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane at the level of the dentate line forms an abscess, which discharges and leaves a persistent epithelialising or granulating track between the internal opening in the anal canal and an external opening on the perianal skin. The course of the track relative to the internal and external anal sphincters determines its classification and surgical difficulty. Secondary tracks and horseshoe extensions can develop. A minority result from specific conditions such as Crohn disease, tuberculosis, pelvic sepsis, radiation, or malignancy, which alter management and prognosis.
additionalInvestigations: Examination under anaesthesia to define the tracks and internal opening
MRI of the pelvis for complex or recurrent fistulae
Endoanal ultrasound to map tracks and sphincter involvement
Colonoscopy or ileocolonoscopy when Crohn disease is suspected
Biopsy of atypical or non-healing tracks to exclude malignancy or tuberculosis
Anorectal physiology and continence assessment when division of sphincter is contemplated
redFlags: Spreading perianal sepsis, cellulitis, or features of necrotising infection (Fournier gangrene) requiring emergency surgery
Systemic sepsis from an undrained abscess
Suspicion of underlying malignancy in a chronic, indurated, or non-healing fistula
Extensive or multiple complex tracks suggesting Crohn disease with risk to continence
reference.prognosis: Simple low fistulae have a high cure rate after laying open with preservation of continence, whereas complex, high, or recurrent tracks carry greater risk of recurrence and incontinence and often require staged, sphincter-preserving strategies. Fistulae associated with Crohn disease are more difficult to heal and tend to recur, and outcomes depend on control of the underlying disease.
pitfalls: Dividing significant sphincter muscle and causing incontinence, particularly in anterior fistulae in women or high tracks
Missing a secondary track or the true internal opening, leading to early recurrence
Laying open a fistula in a patient with undiagnosed Crohn disease with poor healing
Treating an abscess without recognising or planning for an underlying fistula
Failing to biopsy a chronic, atypical, or non-healing track and missing malignancy
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Map the track with examination under anaesthesia, MRI or endoanal ultrasound before definitive surgery
Lay open low, simple tracks by fistulotomy where sphincter involvement is minimal
Use sphincter-preserving techniques such as a seton, the LIFT procedure, an advancement flap or a fistula plug for high or complex tracks to protect continence
Place a draining seton to control sepsis before definitive repair
Treat Crohn-related fistulae medically with anti-tumour-necrosis-factor biologics alongside surgical drainage
Investigate and treat underlying Crohn disease, tuberculosis or malignancy in atypical tracks
Assess anorectal physiology and continence before dividing any sphincter muscle
Refer to colorectal surgery for co-ordinated management
